summary: Gives recommendations for using TLS in XMPP. It updates RFC 6120 and aims to make connections between clients and servers and between servers more secure.

eli5.summary: Advice for locking the chat app's connections, for both users and servers.

questions: should xmpp servers authenticate each other
subtitle: Updates XMPP's TLS rules: follow the current TLS best practices, and do not trust a server that fails to advertise TLS.

tldr.problem: XMPP has used TLS since 1999, but the threat model on the Internet has evolved, so the older recommendations in RFC 6120 and RFC 3920 needed to be stronger.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7590 says XMPP implementations and deployments MUST follow RFC 7525, and adds XMPP-specific advice on STARTTLS, compression, session resumption, authentication, Server Name Indication and user-facing information.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 6120, whose core TLS and certificate rules still apply, and pushes both client-to-server and server-to-server connections toward stronger and more visible encryption.

today: RFC 7590 is a Proposed Standard from June 2015 that updates RFC 6120. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why XMPP Needed Stronger TLS Rules
sections.content:
The Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) and its precursor, the Jabber protocol, have used Transport Layer Security (TLS) and its precursor SSL since 1999. RFC 6120 and its predecessor RFC 3920 both gave advice on TLS. To address the evolving threat model on the Internet, RFC 7590 gives stronger recommendations.

The key rule is that XMPP implementations and deployments MUST follow the best current practices in RFC 7525. Those cover protocol versions, fallback to lower versions, TLS-layer compression, session resumption, cipher suites, public key lengths, forward secrecy and more. The RFC includes them by reference and mostly adds supplementary XMPP-specific information.
sections.eli5: The old advice about locking the chat door was fine long ago. Now there are cleverer burglars, so the rules are tougher.

sections.title: Support for TLS and Stripped Features
sections.content:
Support for TLS, specifically the XMPP profile of STARTTLS, is already mandatory for XMPP implementations. A server normally signals TLS support with a <starttls/> stream feature, and a <required/> child says TLS is mandatory. An attacker could strip either of these out.

So the initiating entity (a client or a peer server) MUST NOT be deterred from attempting TLS even when the receiving entity does not advertise it. Instead it SHOULD, based on local policy, proceed with stream negotiation and try to negotiate TLS.
sections.eli5: If the door does not say it has a lock, try the lock anyway. Someone might have covered the sign.

sections.title: Compression, Resumption and Server Name Indication
sections.content:
XMPP has an application-layer compression extension (XEP-0138). It may have slightly stronger security properties than TLS-layer compression because it is enabled after SASL authentication, but the RFC neither encourages nor discourages its use.

For session resumption, many clients and servers implement stream management (XEP-0198), which resumes XMPP streams at the application layer. Resuming at the TLS layer as well further optimizes the process. Either way, implementations MUST follow RFC 7525 on TLS-layer resumption.

The TLS Server Name Indication extension does no harm but is not necessary, because the to address of the initial stream header serves the same function.
sections.eli5: When you come back to a chat, you can skip some of the paperwork, as long as you still follow the safety rules. And you do not need to say whose house you are visiting twice.

sections.title: Authenticated Connections
sections.content:
RFC 7590 does not replace the certificate validation rules in RFC 6120 or RFC 6125. It restates the goal of preferring authenticated connections:

  • Clients MUST authenticate servers.
  • Servers MUST authenticate clients.
  • Servers SHOULD authenticate other servers.

Server-to-server authentication is only a SHOULD because in multi-tenanted environments it can be extremely difficult to obtain and deploy PKIX certificates with the proper Subject Alternative Names. The Domain Name Associations framework describes other methods, including DANE and PKIX over Secure HTTP (POSH).

Given the pervasiveness of eavesdropping, the RFC says even an encrypted but unauthenticated connection might be better than an unencrypted one. Examples include anonymous Diffie-Hellman and self-signed certificates. Servers may reasonably accept such connections when Server Dialback keys are used, which give only weak identity verification.
sections.eli5: It is best to check the other side's ID card. If you cannot, talking in a whisper is still better than shouting in the street.

sections.title: Human Factors
sections.content:
The RFC strongly encourages clients to let end users, and servers to let administrators, do the following:

  • See whether a stream is encrypted with TLS.
  • See the TLS version used.
  • See how an authenticated connection was verified, such as PKI, DANE, POSH or Server Dialback.
  • Inspect the certificate a server offered.
  • See the cipher suite in use.
  • Be warned if a server's certificate changes.
sections.eli5: The chat app should be able to show you whether the lock is on, what kind it is, and warn you if it suddenly changes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TLS limits the information available to correlate the XMPP layer with the network layers beneath it. Because XMPP typically has just one hop between any two servers, encrypting every hop (sender's client to server, server to server, recipient's server to client) helps limit metadata leakage.

If servers or clients are compromised, per-hop encryption does not protect communications. Even end-to-end encryption of parts of the payload would leave addressing information and roster data in the clear. The document assumes servers and clients have not been subject to widespread compromise. It covers only communication within the XMPP network, not gateways to other networks such as SIP.
sections.eli5: Locking each hallway helps hide who is talking to whom. But if a building itself is taken over, the locks cannot help.
